title.rendered: Biblical Hebrew IV: Advanced Reading Seminar—Kohelet’s Meaning of Life (afternoon)

content.rendered:
Biblical Hebrew IV: Advanced Reading Seminar—Kohelet’s Meaning of Life (afternoon)

An Online Course with Dr. David Zev Moster 
Nine Thursdays: February 11, 25; March 4, 11, 18, 25; April 1, 8, 15, 2026 
2:00–3:30 p.m. ET    

Register Now

We also offer a Thursday morning class from 10:00–11:30 a.m. ET.    

Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) has strong opinions about work, pleasure, time, and life and death. At the heart of the book is the word הֶבֶל (hevel), translated variously as “futile,” “worthless,” “beyond grasp,” and even “absurd.” What does Kohelet mean by it, and how does it shape his understanding of life? 

In nine live online sessions, we will read Kohelet 1–6, focusing on its most challenging verses and exploring multiple possibilities for translation and interpretation. Participants will be encouraged to develop and share their own translations and interpretations of this distinctive work in the Ketuvim (Writings). 

Prerequisite: Completion of Biblical Hebrew I, II, and III. If you have not taken these courses but believe you have the equivalent background, please schedule a conversation with the instructor prior to enrollment.   

Register Now

Cost: $575

Earn a 10% DISCOUNT on courses by declaring your candidacy for the new Certificate in Biblical Hebrew. Complete the four-course sequence and optional capstone project. By the conclusion of the program, you will be able to read and understand a book of the Bible from start to finish in the original Hebrew.   

Learn about the Certificate in Biblical Hebrew

He is the author of Etrog: How a Chinese Fruit Became a Jewish Symbol (2018). He received his PhD from Bar-Ilan University, an MA from New York University and BA, MA, MS, and rabbinic ordination from Yeshiva University.

title.rendered: Introduction to Classical Judeo-Arabic

content.rendered:
Introduction to Classical Judeo-Arabic

An Online Course with Dr. Yaara Perlman 
Ten Thursdays: February 4, 11, 18, 25; March 4, 11, 18, 25; April 1, 8, 2027 
12:00-1:30 p.m. ET   

REGISTER NOW

Beginning with a brief overview of the history and linguistic features of Judeo-Arabic and a survey of major medieval writers, this course will primarily focus on the close reading of texts from a range of genres. Readings will include excerpts from Saadia Gaon’s translation of the Torah and from the Responsa of Maimonides, as well as documentary materials such as private letters and legal documents that are part of JTS’ permanent collection. As such, the course will also offer a window into the lives of medieval Arabic-speaking Jews, illustrating how they engaged with Arabic culture while preserving and developing a unique religious and intellectual heritage 

Prerequisites: This course requires prior knowledge of Arabic, equivalent to 3-4 semesters of university study. Students are also expected to be familiar with Hebrew script by the second week of class. 

Recordings will be available for those unable to attend a session. Space is limited. 

Cost: $650 

REGISTER NOW

About the Instructor

Dr. Yaara Perlman is a historian of the premodern Middle East, working at the intersection of kinship ties created through women, tribal affiliations, and social and political networks. Her research covers topics pertaining to pre-Islamic Arabia, as well as to the early history of Islam from the time of the Prophet Muḥammad to the period of the early ʿAbbāsid caliphs. Her first book, currently in progress, examines Muḥammad’s administrative appointments in the Jewish oasis of Khaybar to shed light on his and his companions’ relationships with the Jews. She holds a Ph.D. from Princeton University and has been a postdoctoral fellow at Tel Aviv University and Yale Law School.

 Learn to read Biblical Hebrew consonants and vowels with confidence. Begin with the Alef Bet and end by reciting entire passages.

Would you like to read the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) in the original but do not know the Hebrew alphabet? In nine live online sessions, you will learn about each of the consonants and vowels, as well as many of the special circumstances that affect pronunciation. The course will introduce you to a variety of resources to aid your progress, including Accordance Bible Software, Dr. David Moster’s Tanakh Cards, MP3 recordings, and interactive online tools. Each session will consist of an instructor-led lesson as well as in-class reading exercises designed to build your skills and support your self-study. You will be encouraged to complete a weekly reading assignment outside of class. 

Upon completion of this course, you will be ready to enroll in Biblical Hebrew I: Jumpstart Your Biblical Hebrew. 

Recordings will be available for those unable to attend a session. Space is limited. 

If you’re not sure whether this course is right for you or if you have additional questions, schedule an appointment to speak with Dr. David Moster, Director of Biblical Hebrew Instruction.

Can you read passages in the Tanakh on your own but lack the confidence to translate some of the more advanced verbal forms in the Qal stem, including commands and wishes, the “flipping Vav,” infinitives, and participles? In eight live online sessions, we will read and workshop passages selected by the instructor and participants, using a variety of resources including Accordance Bible Software1 and Dr. Moster’s Tanakh cards. About Dr. David C. Kraemer and Cantor Magda Fishman

Dr. David C. Kraemer has been part of the JTS community since 1977 when he enrolled at The Graduate School after completing his undergraduate degree at Brandeis University.

He began teaching as a graduate student in 1980, receiving his PhD in 1984. Dr. Kraemer’s focus as a professor is on the literary analysis of rabbinic literature, rabbinic ritual, the social and religious history of Jews in late antiquity, and Jewish diaspora ideologies. He accepted the position of Librarian in 2004 and played a crucial role in forging policy and expanding the impact of The Library’s world-renowned collections and programs.

Dr. Kraemer is a prolific author and commentator. In addition to his books, he has written influential articles on the biblical books of Ezra and Nehemiah, the Mishnah, and other subjects, along with a commentary on Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians (in The Jewish Annotated New Testament, 2nd and 3rd editions). His most recent book, Embracing Exile: The Case for Jewish Diaspora (Oxford University Press, 2025), was named one of “The Best Books of 2025” by The New Yorker.

Cantor Magda Fishman, Senior Cantor of B’nai Torah Congregation in Boca Raton, Florida, is an internationally acclaimed vocalist, musician, and dynamic performer whose extraordinary talent and magnetic stage presence have captivated audiences around the world.

A graduate of the H. L. Miller Cantorial School at the Jewish Theological Seminary, Cantor Fishman is celebrated for her remarkable vocal range, musical versatility, and unique ability to move effortlessly between Broadway, jazz, Israeli music, contemporary favorites, and traditional Jewish melodies. An accomplished trumpet player as well as a gifted singer, she brings an exciting and distinctive dimension to every performance.

Cantor Fishman is also a member of the Folksbiene Yiddish Theatre’s Soul to Soul ensemble, where she celebrates the richness, beauty, and emotional power of Yiddish music and culture.

From prestigious concert halls to intimate musical gatherings, Cantor Fishman combines breathtaking artistry with warmth, humor, and infectious energy. Her passion for music and her extraordinary connection with audiences transform every concert into an unforgettable celebration of music, joy, and the human spirit.

title.rendered: Ask Us Anything: The MFA @ JTS

content.rendered:
Ask Us Anything: The MFA @ JTS 

A Really OPEN Open House

Monday, November 9, 2026
12:00 p.m. ET
Online

The Dean, Director, and Core Faculty Member answer ALL your questions about the JTS MFA in Creative Writing. Join Dr. Lisa Springer, Etgar Keret, and Rachel Kadish for a discussion about the program and all it offers as we kick off the 2027 Admission cycle. This a great chance to discover: 

  • What happens when your writing life becomes part of a community?  
  • What happens when you give writers permission to be weird?  
  • Can I be a writer and still have a day job?  
  • Can I skip the MFA and just get the book deal? 

This session will be recorded and shared with registrants.

REGISTER NOW

About the Speakers

Dr. Lisa Springer serves as Dean of the Division of Lifelong and Professional Studies (DLPS) and Associate Provost for Continuing and Digital Learning. In this role, she leads efforts to expand and innovate JTS’s education for learners at all life stages—whether they seek personal enrichment, professional development, or leadership opportunities. Through DLPS, she oversees programs that extend JTS’s world-class scholarship beyond traditional degree programs, making the institution’s learning more accessible, flexible, and relevant to today’s world.  

Etgar Keret is one of the foremost writers of contemporary Israeli literature. His books have been published in some fifty languages and won numerous awards. In addition to being an internationally acclaimed virtuoso of the short story, Etgar explores a variety of storytelling techniques, including plays, screenplays, songs, animated and live-action films, comic books and choreography. Etgar is an Associate Professor at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. He is excited to guide the JTS MFA program’s vision and mentor emerging storytellers.  

Rachel Kadish is an award-winning fiction writer and essayist. Her work has been read on National Public Radio and has appeared in The New York Times,  Paris Review, and Ploughshares; her most recent novel, The Weight of Ink, was a U.S.A. Today bestseller and recipient of a National Jewish Book Award. She has been a fellow of the National Endowment for the Arts, Radcliffe’s Bunting Institute, the Bellagio Center, and the Bogliasco Foundation, a Koret writer-in-residence at Stanford University, and a Fordham Jewish Studies Fellow at the New York Public Library.

title.rendered: What Comes Next? Jewish Life and the Future We Are Building

content.rendered:
What Comes Next? Jewish Life and the Future We Are Building 

Part of Our Fall 2026 Learning Series, Back to the Future: Jewish Perspectives on What Comes Next

November 30, 2026
Online
1:00–2:10 p.m. ET

With Rabbi Mike Uram, Chancellor, JTS

What might the future of Jewish life look like and what role can we play in shaping it? JTS Chancellor Mike Uram considers the forces shaping Jewish life today and reflects on the choices, opportunities, and questions that may shape its future. 

REGISTER HERE

If you have previously registered for another session in this series, your registration admits you to all sessions in the series, and you may attend as many as you’d like. 

About the Speaker

Rabbi Mike Uram is the ninth Chancellor of The Jewish Theological Seminary and a nationally recognized leader in Jewish learning, engagement, and innovation. The author of the National Jewish Book Award–winning Next Generation Judaism, he has spent his career exploring how Jewish organizations can reinvent themselves to meet the needs of changing communities. Chancellor Uram focuses on new approaches to Jewish engagement and on breaking down the boundaries that can prevent people from developing full and meaningful Jewish identities. 

About the Series

Preoccupation with what comes next, especially in periods of uncertainty, is hardly a new phenomenon. Looking ahead—to what might change, what might endure, and what might be possible—runs throughout Jewish text and tradition.

In this series, JTS scholars and alumni look backward and forward, exploring how Jews across centuries have imagined what comes next, prepared for the unknown, and established what they hoped would endure. From biblical visions and rabbinic ideas about the world to come to preservation, artificial intelligence, and the future of Jewish life, we’ll ask not only what the future might hold, but how we can help shape it.

title.rendered: Preserving the Past in Service of the Future: A History of The JTS Library

content.rendered:
Preserving the Past in Service of the Future: A History of The JTS Library 

Part of Our Fall 2026 Learning Series, Back to the Future: Jewish Perspectives on What Comes Next

December 14, 2026
Online
1:00–2:10 p.m. ET

With Dr. Yitz Landes, Assistant Professor of Rabbinic Literatures and Cultures, JTS

The JTS Library was founded to preserve the Jewish textual tradition and to build a resource for generations to come. Dr. Yitz Landes traces this vision from The Library’s founding and the growth of its extraordinary collection through the devastating fire of 1966—the subject of an exhibition he curated, currently on view at JTS—and the decades of rebuilding that followed. Looking at The Library today, from teaching with its collections to making its treasures accessible online, he explores how preservation serves both as an act of memory and an investment in the future. 

REGISTER HERE

If you have previously registered for another session in this series, your registration admits you to all sessions in the series, and you may attend as many as you’d like. 

About the Speaker

title.rendered: The Bikur Cholim Shul in Slovakia: Preparing for the Future

content.rendered:
The Bikur Cholim Shul in Slovakia: Preparing for the Future 

Part of Our Fall 2026 Learning Series, Back to the Future: Jewish Perspectives on What Comes Next

December 7, 2026
Online
1:00–2:10 p.m. ET

With Dr. Marjorie Lehman, Professor of Talmud and Rabbinics, JTS

What can a collection of old books tell us about a community that is no longer there to tell its own story? And what happens when those books remain exactly where that community left them? A few hundred volumes still rest on the shelves of the Bikur Cholim Synagogue in Bardejov, Slovakia, where they have remained since the destruction of the Jewish community in 1942.  

The session will explore the ways that Jewish books can be used to recover the intellectual, religious, and everyday life of Jewish Bardejov before the Holocaust. But it also asks a larger question: What does it mean to preserve a past for a unknown future?

title.rendered: Anticipatory Memory: Remembering the Future

content.rendered:
Anticipatory Memory: Remembering the Future 

Part of Our Fall 2026 Learning Series, Back to the Future: Jewish Perspectives on What Comes Next

November 23, 2026
Online
1:00–2:10 p.m. ET

With Rabbi Gordon Tucker, Vice Chancellor for Religious Life and Engagement, JTS

We usually think of the past as fixed and knowable and the future as uncertain—something we can only predict. Part of being human is not knowing what is coming, while constantly striving to not only know, but also to control the future. Jewish texts offer a surprising possibility: that we can, and perhaps must, “remember” the future.

Drawing on Lamentations, an extraordinary Targumic account of the pascal sacrifice preceding the Exodus, and ideas about the nature of time from Jewish theology to modern physics, Rabbi Gordon Tucker will explore how a vision of the future can shape our choices in the present. What changes when the future is not simply something that happens to us, but something we actively envision—and work toward?

title.rendered: Rabbinic Futures, Short and Long Term

content.rendered:
Rabbinic Futures, Short and Long Term 

Part of Our Fall 2026 Learning Series, Back to the Future: Jewish Perspectives on What Comes Next

November 9, 2026
Online
1:00–2:10 p.m. ET

With Dr. David Kraemer, Gerson D. Cohen Chair in Talmud and Rabbinic Culture, JTS

As time passed following the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE, the rabbis never gave up on the hope of ultimate restoration, continuing to anticipate a long-term future when the anointed king of Judah (the messiah) would be returned to his throne, the Temple rebuilt, and so forth. But while hoping for this future, they simultaneously built a Judaism for the long “short-term,” one that would make it possible for Jews to wait for many generations until the final restoration.

In this session, we will explore this “short-term/long-term” strategy and ask what wisdom it offers for us today.

title.rendered: The Future of Torah: Jewish Learning in the Age of AI

content.rendered:
The Future of Torah: Jewish Learning in the Age of AI 

Part of Our Fall 2026 Learning Series, Back to the Future: Jewish Perspectives on What Comes Next

October 26, 2026
Online
1:00–2:10 p.m. ET

With Rabbi Dr. Zohar Atkins, JTS alum, scholar, writer, and founder of Lightning, a lifelong learning AI platform

Artificial intelligence is transforming how we find, organize, and create knowledge. What could this mean for a Jewish tradition built on centuries of interpretation, debate, and discovery? 

Major technological shifts—from the printing press to digital libraries—have changed the accessibility of Jewish texts and the ways in which we study Torah. Rabbi Zohar Atkins explores AI as the next chapter in that story: a technology that could dramatically expand access to Jewish learning, uncover new connections across centuries of tradition, and create new possibilities for interpretation and insight. Rather than asking what AI might replace, he asks what it might enable—and what kinds of readers, teachers, and communities we might become as we help shape the future of Torah.
